title: The Quid Pro Quo That Wasn’t
text:
The Quid Pro Quo That Wasn’t

Louis-Vincent Gave

Gavekal Research | 27 Jul 2026

In mid-May, and as the Strait of Hormuz closure was entering its 10th week, President Donald Trump hopped over to Beijing for a 72-hour state visit. President Trump was accompanied by many prominent American CEOs of tech, finance and consumer product companies. The list of corporate leaders on the plane gave rise to hopes that China would embrace more financial deregulation, more market opening for US companies, and more cross-border investments. In the end, aside from broad declarations of goodwill, few concrete measures were adopted. Instead, when it came to the stabilization of the Sino-US relationship, cans were kicked firmly down the road to the upcoming September 24 meeting between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Against this backdrop, one important development was the collapse in Chinese oil imports that came through in the May and June trade data. With China essentially walking away from the global seaborne oil market, oil prices failed to reach the heights that most experts predicted would follow the Strait of Hormuz closure (see Lessons Learned And Relearned?).
